claim: Pain induction induces relapse in murine experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model for multiple sclerosis.
source: Here we show using murine experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a model for multiple sclerosis (MS), that pain induces EAE relapse.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Pain induction activates a sensory-sympathetic signal in EAE-recovered mice.
source: Mechanistic analysis showed that pain induction activates a sensory-sympathetic signal followed by a chemokine-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells that showed antigen-presentation activity at specific ventral vessels in the fifth lumbar cord of EAE-recovered mice.
evidence: The abstract describes mechanistic analysis demonstrating this pathway.

claim: Pain induction leads to chemokine-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at specific ventral vessels in the fifth lumbar cord.
source: Mechanistic analysis showed that pain induction activates a sensory-sympathetic signal followed by a chemokine-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells that showed antigen-presentation activity at specific ventral vessels in the fifth lumbar cord of EAE-recovered mice.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from mechanistic analysis.

claim: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells accumulated at L5 ventral vessels show antigen-presentation activity.
source: Mechanistic analysis showed that pain induction activates a sensory-sympathetic signal followed by a chemokine-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells that showed antigen-presentation activity at specific ventral vessels in the fifth lumbar cord of EAE-recovered mice.
evidence: The abstract states these cells showed antigen-presentation activity.

claim: Pathogenic CD4+ T cells are recruited to the spinal cord in a manner dependent on a local chemokine inducer in endothelial cells following MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation.
source: Following this accumulation, various immune cells including pathogenic CD4+ T cells recruited in the spinal cord in a manner dependent on a local chemokine inducer in endothelial cells, resulting in EAE relapse.
evidence: The abstract describes this sequential mechanism.

claim: Multiple sclerosis is genetically a T helper cell (CD4+ T cell)-mediated autoimmune disease.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is genetically a T helper cell (CD4+ T cell)-mediated autoimmune disease (International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium et al., 2011) that is characterized by chronic inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS) and relapse in over two thirds of patients (Steinman, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium et al., 2011.

claim: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by chronic inflammation in the central nervous system.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is genetically a T helper cell (CD4+ T cell)-mediated autoimmune disease (International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium et al., 2011) that is characterized by chronic inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS) and relapse in over two thirds of patients (Steinman, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Steinman, 2009.

claim: Relapse occurs in over two thirds of multiple sclerosis patients.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is genetically a T helper cell (CD4+ T cell)-mediated autoimmune disease (International Multiple Sclerosis Genetics Consortium et al., 2011) that is characterized by chronic inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS) and relapse in over two thirds of patients (Steinman, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Steinman, 2009.

claim: MS relapse is marked by inflammatory lesions consisting of various immune cells including CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and macrophages.
source: Such relapse is marked by inflammatory lesions consisting of various immune cells including CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and macrophages followed by a loss of neurological function in various regions of the CNS (Steinman, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Steinman, 2014.

claim: MS relapse is followed by a loss of neurological function in various regions of the CNS.
source: Such relapse is marked by inflammatory lesions consisting of various immune cells including CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, and macrophages followed by a loss of neurological function in various regions of the CNS (Steinman, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Steinman, 2014.

claim: Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice have been designed to study the molecular mechanisms of MS relapse.
source: To understand the molecular mechanisms involved in the relapse, disease model animals including experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice have been designed to study the corresponding molecular mechanism (Miller et al., 1995; Steinman, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1995 and Steinman, 2009.

claim: A detailed explanation for MS relapse is still lacking.
source: However, a detailed explanation for the relapse is still lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Pain induction is a symptom of multiple sclerosis.
source: Pain induction is a symptom of MS (Thompson et al., 2010) and sometimes a determinant of MS activity (Ehde et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2010.

claim: Pain induction is sometimes a determinant of MS activity.
source: Pain induction is a symptom of MS (Thompson et al., 2010) and sometimes a determinant of MS activity (Ehde et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ehde et al., 2003.

claim: Pain induction is commonly interpreted as a biomarker of inflammation.
source: Pain induction is commonly interpreted as a biomarker of inflammation, although inflammation can sometimes occur in the CNS without it (Watson et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a common interpretation, with a citation to Watson et al., 1991 for the exception.

claim: Inflammation can sometimes occur in the CNS without pain.
source: Pain induction is commonly interpreted as a biomarker of inflammation, although inflammation can sometimes occur in the CNS without it (Watson et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Watson et al., 1991.

claim: A correlation between pain intensity and the pathogenesis of inflammation is poorly established and still debated.
source: Yet a correlation between pain intensity and the pathogenesis of inflammation is poorly established and still debated (Beiske et al., 2004; Kalia and O'Connor, 2005; Solaro et al., 2004; Ehde et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beiske et al., 2004; Kalia and O'Connor, 2005; Solaro et al., 2004; Ehde et al., 2006.

claim: It has not been demonstrated whether pain induction is involved in MS relapse.
source: More specifically, it has not been demonstrated whether pain induction is involved in MS relapse.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The inflammation amplifier is a local chemokine inducer in non-immune cells.
source: One critical machinery for inflammation development is a local chemokine inducer in non-immune cells termed the inflammation amplifier (formerly IL-6 amplifier), which we originally discovered in several disease models including EAE (Ogura et al., 2008; Hirano, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogura et al., 2008 and Hirano, 2010.

claim: The inflammation amplifier was originally discovered in several disease models including EAE.
source: One critical machinery for inflammation development is a local chemokine inducer in non-immune cells termed the inflammation amplifier (formerly IL-6 amplifier), which we originally discovered in several disease models including EAE (Ogura et al., 2008; Hirano, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogura et al., 2008 and Hirano, 2010.

claim: The inflammation amplifier involves massive chemokine expression caused by the simultaneous stimulation of NFkB and STAT3.
source: In this system, massive chemokine expression caused by the simultaneous stimulation of NFkB and STAT3 is followed by disruption of local homeostasis due to the local accumulation of various immune cells (Murakami and Hirano, 2011; Murakami et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Murakami and Hirano, 2011; Murakami et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012, 2013.

claim: Activation of the inflammation amplifier is followed by disruption of local homeostasis due to the local accumulation of various immune cells.
source: In this system, massive chemokine expression caused by the simultaneous stimulation of NFkB and STAT3 is followed by disruption of local homeostasis due to the local accumulation of various immune cells (Murakami and Hirano, 2011; Murakami et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Murakami and Hirano, 2011; Murakami et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012, 2013.

claim: Activation of the inflammation amplifier is associated with many human diseases including autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases such as MS.
source: Activation of the inflammation amplifier is associated with many human diseases and disorders such as autoimmune and neurodegenerative diseases including MS (Murakami et al., 2013; Atsumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Murakami et al., 2013 and Atsumi et al., 2014.

claim: Gateways for pathogenic CD4+ T cells in an EAE model have been established by activation of the inflammation amplifier via an anti-gravity-mediated regional neural signal in the fifth lumbar cord (L5).
source: Gateways for pathogenic CD4+ T cells in an EAE model have been established by activation of the inflammation amplifier via an anti-gravity-mediated regional neural signal in the fifth lumbar cord (L5) (Arima et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Arima et al., 2012 and Mori et al., 2014.

claim: Soleus muscle-mediated sensory-sympathetic neural signals enhance inflammation amplifier activation in L5 dorsal vessels via local norepinephrine expression derived from sympathetic neurons.
source: Soleus muscle-mediated sensory-sympathetic neural signals enhance inflammation amplifier activation in L5 dorsal vessels via local norepinephrine expression derived from sympathetic neurons to create gates through which immune cells reach the CNS and cause inflammation there (Arima et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Arima et al., 2012.

claim: Gates for immune cell entry into the CNS can be artificially manipulated via the activation of local neural signals by electrically stimulating muscles.
source: These gates can be artificially manipulated via the activation of local neural signals by electrically stimulating muscles, resulting in an accumulation of immune cells in the intended regions (Arima et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Arima et al., 2012.

claim: The gateway reflex is an example of neural signaling-mediated regulation of inflammation.
source: Gating blood vessels by regional neural stimulations, a phenomenon termed the gateway reflex, is an example of the neural signaling-mediated regulation of inflammation (Tracey, 2012; Sabharwal et al., 2014) and has potential therapeutic value not only in preventing autoimmunity, but also in augmenting the effects of immunotherapies against infections and cancers (Ogura et al., 2013; Atsumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tracey, 2012 and Sabharwal et al., 2014.

claim: The gateway reflex has potential therapeutic value in preventing autoimmunity and augmenting the effects of immunotherapies against infections and cancers.
source: Gating blood vessels by regional neural stimulations, a phenomenon termed the gateway reflex, is an example of the neural signaling-mediated regulation of inflammation (Tracey, 2012; Sabharwal et al., 2014) and has potential therapeutic value not only in preventing autoimmunity, but also in augmenting the effects of immunotherapies against infections and cancers (Ogura et al., 2013; Atsumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ogura et al., 2013 and Atsumi et al., 2014.

claim: Neural activations are induced by various situations including pain.
source: Because it is known that neural activations are induced by various situations including pain (Delmas et al., 2011; Palazzo et al., 2012; LaMotte et al., 2014), we considered whether neural signals mediated by pain induction plays a role in the pathogenesis of EAE relapse via the gating of certain blood vessels.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Delmas et al., 2011; Palazzo et al., 2012; LaMotte et al., 2014.

claim: EAE was induced within 1 week after passive transfer of pathogenic CD4+ T cells and disappeared at about 2–3 weeks after the transfer.
source: EAE was induced within 1 week and disappeared at about 2–3 weeks after the transfer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No relapse was found even more than 300 days after pathogenic T cell transfer in the passive transfer EAE model.
source: In contrast, we found no relapse even more than 300 days after the pathogenic T cell transfer (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The C57BL/6 mouse strain lacks natural relapses in EAE.
source: Consistent with these results, it is known that the lack of natural relapses in the C57BL/6 mouse strain.
evidence: This is stated as known information.

claim: Pain induction on the same day of T cell transfer did not accelerate disease development during the onset period (until 10 days after transfer).
source: Although this pain induction did not accelerate disease development, particularly during the onset period (until 10 days after the pathogenic T cell transfer), the pain persisted and maintained symptoms at a high level from 15 days post T cell transfer compared with sham mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pain induction maintained EAE symptoms at a high level from 15 days post T cell transfer compared with sham mice.
source: Although this pain induction did not accelerate disease development, particularly during the onset period (until 10 days after the pathogenic T cell transfer), the pain persisted and maintained symptoms at a high level from 15 days post T cell transfer compared with sham mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pain induction itself (without pathogenic T cell transfer) did not induce the development of EAE.
source: We found that pain induction itself (without pathogenic T cell transfer) did not induce the development of EAE (Figure 1B) and that pain induced in mice with pathogenic T cells gradually caused a low clinical score over 20 days after the transfer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EAE-recovered mice have negligible cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area.
source: We found negligible cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area, which is a key area involved in pain sensation (Li et al., 2010), in the brain of EAE-recovered mice and negligible pain sensation according to the von Frey test of the extremity, trunk of the body, face, head (Figure 1C and data not shown), suggesting that remittent mice have minimal pain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C, with citation to Li et al., 2010 for the role of the somatosensory area.

claim: EAE-recovered mice have negligible pain sensation according to the von Frey test.
source: We found negligible cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area, which is a key area involved in pain sensation (Li et al., 2010), in the brain of EAE-recovered mice and negligible pain sensation according to the von Frey test of the extremity, trunk of the body, face, head (Figure 1C and data not shown), suggesting that remittent mice have minimal pain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Remittent mice have minimal pain.
source: We found negligible cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area, which is a key area involved in pain sensation (Li et al., 2010), in the brain of EAE-recovered mice and negligible pain sensation according to the von Frey test of the extremity, trunk of the body, face, head (Figure 1C and data not shown), suggesting that remittent mice have minimal pain.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on cfos expression and von Frey test results.

claim: Pain induction in EAE-recovered mice resulted in a relapse of EAE.
source: Then we investigated whether pain induction was involved in the relapse of EAE. We induced pain in EAE-recovered mice that had developed transient EAE. Pain induction resulted in a relapse of EAE (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gabapentin suppressed the development of EAE relapse after pain induction.
source: Pain medicines such as Gabapentin and/or Pregabalin, which reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area or von Frey test values after pain-induction (data not shown), suppressed the development of EAE relapse (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Pregabalin suppressed the development of EAE relapse after pain induction.
source: Pain medicines such as Gabapentin and/or Pregabalin, which reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area or von Frey test values after pain-induction (data not shown), suppressed the development of EAE relapse (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Gabapentin and Pregabalin reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain-induction.
source: Pain medicines such as Gabapentin and/or Pregabalin, which reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area or von Frey test values after pain-induction (data not shown), suppressed the development of EAE relapse (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Capsaicin injected into the whiskers or forefeet caused EAE relapse.
source: On the other hand, capsaicin, a painful agent, injected into the whiskers or forefeet caused EAE relapse (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A relapsing-remittent model of SJL/PLP mice was suppressed by pain medicines.
source: A relapsing-remittent model of SJL/PLP mice was also suppressed by pain medicines (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Activated neurons in trigeminal ganglions expressed the sensory markers TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8 after pain induction.
source: Activated neurons, as defined by NeuN and cfos expressions, expressed the sensory markers TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8 in trigeminal ganglions.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Negligible cfos expression was found in sensory marker-expressing neurons in the absence of ligation in the remittent phase.
source: We found negligible cfos expression, however, in the subtypes of these markers in the absence of ligation in the remittent phase (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: cfos+-activated neurons also expressed TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8 in trigeminal ganglions after pain induction.
source: Immunohistochemical experiments using serial sections showed that cfos+-activated neurons also expressed TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with a Nav1.8 blocker, A803467, suppressed the development of the EAE relapse.
source: Treatment with a Nav1.8 blocker, A803467, suppressed the development of the EAE relapse (Figure 2C), and TRPV1-deficient hosts showed suppressed relapse (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TRPV1-deficient hosts showed suppressed EAE relapse after pain induction.
source: Treatment with a Nav1.8 blocker, A803467, suppressed the development of the EAE relapse (Figure 2C), and TRPV1-deficient hosts showed suppressed relapse (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Animals treated with A803467 showed reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain-induction.
source: We also found that animals treated with A803467 and TRPV1-deficient hosts showed reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area or low von Frey values after pain-induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right panels and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRPV1-deficient hosts showed reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain-induction.
source: We also found that animals treated with A803467 and TRPV1-deficient hosts showed reduced cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area or low von Frey values after pain-induction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right panels and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ligation of the facial nerves induced negligible development of EAE relapse.
source: Moreover, ligation of the facial nerves, which mainly contain motor nerves and the vagus nerves, which mainly contain efferent fibers such as parasympathetic and motor nerves to various viscera induced negligible development of EAE relapse (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ligation of the vagus nerves induced negligible development of EAE relapse.
source: Moreover, ligation of the facial nerves, which mainly contain motor nerves and the vagus nerves, which mainly contain efferent fibers such as parasympathetic and motor nerves to various viscera induced negligible development of EAE relapse (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of sensory pathways are involved in the pain-induced relapse.
source: Therefore, we concluded that the activation of sensory pathways are involved in the pain-induced relapse.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Blood flow speed was faster in pain-induced than sham-operated mice in various blood vessels including L5 and L1 dorsal vessels.
source: We first investigated blood flow speed, which is controlled by autonomic neurons including sympathetic ones, in the dorsal vessels of L5 and L1, the bottoms of the forefeet, the hindlimb, femoral vessels, and brain surface vessels in pain-induced mice. Blood flow speed was faster in pain-induced than sham-operated mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sympathetic activation affects blood vessels in the CNS after pain induction.
source: These results suggested that sympathetic activation affects blood vessels in the CNS after pain induction.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the blood flow speed results.

claim: Neurons of the somatosensory area, particularly the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), were activated according to cfos expression after pain induction.
source: Consistent with these results, neurons of the somatosensory area, particularly the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), where sensory nerves are localized with autonomic nerves including sympathetic ones (Ikemoto et al., 1999; Critchley, 2005), were activated according to cfos expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C, with citations to Ikemoto et al., 1999 and Critchley, 2005.

claim: Sympathetic ganglions were activated after pain induction, with the activation status in L5 being higher than in other cords.
source: Moreover, sympathetic ganglions were activated after pain induction, with the activation status in L5 being higher than in other cords (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with atenolol, an inhibitor of the norepinephrine β1 receptor, significantly suppressed the relapse development.
source: Furthermore, treatment with atenolol, an inhibitor of the norepinephrine β1 receptor, significantly suppressed the relapse development (Figure 3C), and treatment with 6-OHDA, which induces sympathectomy, suppressed the EAE relapse (Figure 3D), while mice treated with atenolol and 6-OHDA did not suppress cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with 6-OHDA, which induces sympathectomy, suppressed the EAE relapse.
source: Furthermore, treatment with atenolol, an inhibitor of the norepinephrine β1 receptor, significantly suppressed the relapse development (Figure 3C), and treatment with 6-OHDA, which induces sympathectomy, suppressed the EAE relapse (Figure 3D), while mice treated with atenolol and 6-OHDA did not suppress cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mice treated with atenolol and 6-OHDA did not suppress cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction.
source: Furthermore, treatment with atenolol, an inhibitor of the norepinephrine β1 receptor, significantly suppressed the relapse development (Figure 3C), and treatment with 6-OHDA, which induces sympathectomy, suppressed the EAE relapse (Figure 3D), while mice treated with atenolol and 6-OHDA did not suppress cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: EAE mice under immobilization stress or forced swimming did not show EAE relapse.
source: Moreover, EAE mice under immobilization stress or forced swimming did not show EAE relapse, although these conditions did increase serum corticosterone, norepinephrine, and epinephrine similarly to pain induction (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Immobilization stress and forced swimming increased serum corticosterone, norepinephrine, and epinephrine similarly to pain induction.
source: Moreover, EAE mice under immobilization stress or forced swimming did not show EAE relapse, although these conditions did increase serum corticosterone, norepinephrine, and epinephrine similarly to pain induction (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Specific sympathetic pathways triggered by pain induction, but not pain-mediated systemic hormonal responses and/or stress-mediated events, play a role in the development of EAE relapse.
source: Therefore, these data suggest specific sympathetic pathways triggered by pain induction, but not pain-mediated systemic hormonal responses and/or stress-mediated events, play a role in the development of EAE relapse.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Many cell populations increased in the L5 cord after pain induction, especially CD11b+ cells and particularly MHC class II+ ones, in EAE-recovered mice.
source: Many cell populations increased in the L5 cord after pain induction (Figure 4A), especially those of CD11b+ cells and particularly MHC class II+ ones, in EAE-recovered mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The accumulated CD4+ T cells in early phase (day 1–2) after pain induction were mainly Th17 cells.
source: Furthermore, the accumulated CD4+ T cells in early phase (day 1–2) after pain induction were mainly Th17 cells, while in later time points (day 5 and later) after pain induction, we found not only other helper subset in L5 cord and lymphocytes accumulations in several regions of brain just like primary EAE responses (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The majority of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of EAE remittent hosts originated from peripheral monocytes but not resident microglial cells.
source: We found similar percentages of CD45.1+ cells and peripheral derived CD45.2+ cells in MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of EAE remittent parabiosis hosts, while MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of wild type parabiosis mice had only a low number of CD45.1+ cells (Figure 4B). These results suggested that the majority of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of EAE remittent hosts originated from peripheral monocytes but not resident microglial cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pain induction resulted in a strong accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord, particularly at the ventral vessels.
source: Pain induction resulted in a strong accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord, particularly at the ventral vessels (Figure 4C, ligation).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Depletion of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the cisterna magna suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at L5 ventral vessels and the relapse development after pain induction.
source: Moreover, depletion of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the cisterna magna but not in the peritoneal cavity suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at L5 ventral vessels and the relapse development after pain induction (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Depletion of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the peritoneal cavity did not suppress the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at L5 ventral vessels and the relapse development after pain induction.
source: Moreover, depletion of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the cisterna magna but not in the peritoneal cavity suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at L5 ventral vessels and the relapse development after pain induction (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells, which were likely derived from the CNS side, at the L5 ventral vessels is important for EAE relapse.
source: These results demonstrated that the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells, which were likely derived from the CNS side, at the L5 ventral vessels is important for EAE relapse.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the depletion experiments.

claim: MK801, an antagonist of NMDA receptors, injected to the ACC suppressed the expression of cfos and the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord after pain induction.
source: We found an antagonist of NMDA receptors, MK801, injected to the ACC not only suppressed the expression of cfos but also the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord after pain induction (Figure 4E), while an agonist of NMDA receptors, L-Homocysteic acid, injected to the ACC enhanced the expression of cfos and the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord without ligation of the trigeminal nerves (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: L-Homocysteic acid, an agonist of NMDA receptors, injected to the ACC enhanced the expression of cfos and the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord without ligation of the trigeminal nerves.
source: We found an antagonist of NMDA receptors, MK801, injected to the ACC not only suppressed the expression of cfos but also the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord after pain induction (Figure 4E), while an agonist of NMDA receptors, L-Homocysteic acid, injected to the ACC enhanced the expression of cfos and the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels in the L5 cord without ligation of the trigeminal nerves (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The pain-mediated neural activation was at least in part dependent on the ACC.
source: These results suggested that the pain-mediated neural activation was at least in part dependent on the ACC.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the MK801 and L-Homocysteic acid experiments.

claim: TH + sympathetic nerves were innervated around L5 ventral vessels.
source: TH + sympathetic nerves were innervated and Creb molecules, a transcriptional factor of norepinephrine, were activated around L5 ventral vessels (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Creb molecules, a transcriptional factor of norepinephrine, were activated around L5 ventral vessels.
source: TH + sympathetic nerves were innervated and Creb molecules, a transcriptional factor of norepinephrine, were activated around L5 ventral vessels (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Chemokine expression was found around the ventral vessels after pain induction.
source: We also found chemokine expression around the ventral vessels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with atenolol suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells but not cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction.
source: Treatment with atenolol and 6-OHDA-mediated sympathectomy suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells but not cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction (Figure 5D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6-OHDA-mediated sympathectomy suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells but not cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction.
source: Treatment with atenolol and 6-OHDA-mediated sympathectomy suppressed the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells but not cfos expression in neurons of the somatosensory area after pain induction (Figure 5D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of CX3CR1 molecules was increased on MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice.
source: To identify which specific chemokines are involved in the sympathetic-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord, we first investigated the expression of chemokine receptors on MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice, finding that the expression of CX3CR1 molecules and their ligand, CX3CL1, were increased particularly after pain induction (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: CX3CL1 expression was increased particularly after pain induction in EAE-recovered mice.
source: To identify which specific chemokines are involved in the sympathetic-mediated accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord, we first investigated the expression of chemokine receptors on MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice, finding that the expression of CX3CR1 molecules and their ligand, CX3CL1, were increased particularly after pain induction (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: CX3CL1 molecules were found around the L5 ventral vessels.
source: Immunohistochemistry experiments confirmed that CX3CL1 molecules were found around the L5 ventral vessels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Norepinephrine treatment increased CX3CL1 expression in primary CD11b+ cells.
source: Norepinephrine treatment increased CX3CL1 expression in primary CD11b+ cells (Figure 5H), while norepinephrine-mediated CX3CL1 expression was suppressed in CD11b+ cells derived from β1 and β2 receptor-deficient mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Norepinephrine-mediated CX3CL1 expression was suppressed in CD11b+ cells derived from β1 and β2 receptor-deficient mice.
source: Norepinephrine treatment increased CX3CL1 expression in primary CD11b+ cells (Figure 5H), while norepinephrine-mediated CX3CL1 expression was suppressed in CD11b+ cells derived from β1 and β2 receptor-deficient mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Blockade of CX3CL1 by a neutralizing antibody in the CNS significantly suppressed the L5 accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells as well as the relapse development after pain induction.
source: Indeed, blockade of CX3CL1 by a neutralizing antibody in the CNS significantly suppressed the L5 accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells as well as the relapse development after pain induction (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: Pain-mediated CX3CL1 chemokine expression via the sympathetic pathway is critical for the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the L5 ventral vessels of EAE-recovered mice.
source: These results demonstrated that pain-mediated CX3CL1 chemokine expression via the sympathetic pathway is critical for the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the L5 ventral vessels of EAE-recovered mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice expressed MHC class II molecules and costimulatory molecules.
source: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice expressed not only MHC class II molecules but also costimulatory molecules (Figure 6A) and had the ability to stimulate pathogenic CD4+ T cells without the addition of MOG peptide (Figure 6B), suggesting MHC class II+CD11b+ cells presented self-antigen peptides that stimulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice had the ability to stimulate pathogenic CD4+ T cells without the addition of MOG peptide.
source: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice expressed not only MHC class II molecules but also costimulatory molecules (Figure 6A) and had the ability to stimulate pathogenic CD4+ T cells without the addition of MOG peptide (Figure 6B), suggesting MHC class II+CD11b+ cells presented self-antigen peptides that stimulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells presented self-antigen peptides that stimulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
source: MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in EAE-recovered mice expressed not only MHC class II molecules but also costimulatory molecules (Figure 6A) and had the ability to stimulate pathogenic CD4+ T cells without the addition of MOG peptide (Figure 6B), suggesting MHC class II+CD11b+ cells presented self-antigen peptides that stimulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the antigen presentation assay.

claim: Anti-CD4 antibody treatment significantly suppressed the development of the EAE relapse.
source: We then investigated the relationship between MHC class II+CD11b+ cells and pathogenic CD4+ T cells in EAE relapse after pain induction. Anti-CD4 antibody treatment significantly suppressed the development of the EAE relapse (Figure 6C) despite the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Anti-CD4 antibody treatment did not suppress the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at L5 ventral vessels.
source: We then investigated the relationship between MHC class II+CD11b+ cells and pathogenic CD4+ T cells in EAE relapse after pain induction. Anti-CD4 antibody treatment significantly suppressed the development of the EAE relapse (Figure 6C) despite the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Blockades of sympathetic activation and CX3CL1 expression suppressed the accumulation of both MHC class II+CD11b+ cells and pathogenic CD4+ T cells at L5 ventral vessels.
source: Blockades of sympathetic activation and CX3CL1 expression suppressed the accumulation of not only MHC class II+CD11b+ cells, but also pathogenic CD4+ T cells at L5 ventral vessels (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Pain induction first causes an accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels of the L5 cord and then a MHC class II+CD11b+ cell-mediated accumulation and activation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that pain induction first causes an accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the ventral vessels of the L5 cord and then a MHC class II+CD11b+ cell-mediated accumulation and activation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells, the latter being also critical for the development of EAE relapse.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: L5 ventral vessels had increased expressions of various chemokines, including CCL20 and CCL5, in EAE-recovered mice particularly after pain induction.
source: L5 ventral vessels indeed had increased expressions of various chemokines, including CCL20 and CCL5, in EAE-recovered mice particularly after pain induction (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: NFkB and STAT3 molecules were simultaneously activated around L5 vessels after pain induction.
source: NFkB and STAT3 molecules were simultaneously activated around L5 vessels after pain induction (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The blockade of IL-6 suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation.
source: The blockade of IL-6, IL-17A, or CCL20 signaling suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation (Figure 6G–I and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G–I.

claim: The blockade of IL-17A suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation.
source: The blockade of IL-6, IL-17A, or CCL20 signaling suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation (Figure 6G–I and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G–I.

claim: The blockade of CCL20 signaling suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation.
source: The blockade of IL-6, IL-17A, or CCL20 signaling suppressed the pain-mediated accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells as well as the development of the EAE relapse without affecting MHC class II+CD11b+ cell accumulation (Figure 6G–I and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Excess expression of chemokines at L5 ventral vessels is critical for the development of EAE relapse via pathogenic CD4+ T cell accumulation.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that excess expression of chemokines at L5 ventral vessels is critical for the development of EAE relapse via pathogenic CD4+ T cell accumulation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Pain-mediated sympathetic pathways induce relapse following sensory activation in EAE models.
source: We here demonstrated that pain-mediated sympathetic pathways induce relapse following sensory activation in EAE models.
evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Sensory neurons expressing TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8, sensory-sympathetic connections in the ACC, and sympathetic neurons were involved in the pain-induced EAE relapse response.
source: To clarify if the relapse responses were due to neural signals and not pain-mediated systemic hormonal responses or stress-mediated events, we first investigated sensory and sympathetic pathways, finding that sensory neurons expressing TRPV1 and/or Nav1.8, sensory-sympathetic connections in the ACC, and sympathetic neurons were involved in the response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: The relapse responses can be divided into at least four steps.
source: We could divide the relapse responses into at least four steps.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The first step of pain-induced EAE relapse is pain-mediated sensory activation followed by sympathetic activation.
source: The first step is pain-mediated sensory activation followed by sympathetic activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The second step of pain-induced EAE relapse is pain-mediated sympathetic activation that triggers the regional expression of the chemokine CX3CL1 followed by the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the L5 ventral vessels.
source: The second step is pain-mediated sympathetic activation. This activation triggers the regional expression of the chemokine CX3CL1 followed by the accumulation of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at the L5 ventral vessels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The third step for EAE relapse is the accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells at the L5 ventral vessels, which is most likely dependent on self-antigen presentation via MHC class II+CD11b+ cells.
source: The third step for EAE relapse is the accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells at the L5 ventral vessels. This step is most likely dependent on self-antigen presentation via MHC class II+CD11b+ cells, because these cells stimulated MOG-specific pathogenic CD4+ T cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: The fourth and final step of EAE relapse is mediated by excessive chemokine expressions and is most likely triggered by the activation of the accumulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells.
source: The fourth and final step is mediated by excessive chemokine expressions and is most likely triggered by the activation of the accumulated pathogenic CD4+ T cells in the third step.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The number of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells was higher in the L5 cord than other cords, particularly in EAE-recovered mice, even without pain induction.
source: The number of MHC class II+CD11b+ cells was higher in the L5 cord than other cords, particularly in EAE-recovered mice, even without pain induction (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The L5 specificity of the relapse development may be because the L5 cord is the site of initial inflammation and is the tissue most damaged during the primary development of EAE.
source: The L5 specificity of the relapse development may be because the L5 cord is the site of initial inflammation and is the tissue most damaged during the primary development of EAE.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: A low but sufficient level of sympathetic activation may maintain a low level of the inflammation state in the L5 cord to accumulate MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of EAE-recovered mice and develop EAE relapse after pain induction.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that a low but sufficient level of sympathetic activation may maintain a low level of the inflammation state in the L5 cord to accumulate MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in the L5 cord of EAE-recovered mice and develop EAE relapse after pain induction.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion.

claim: Many patients with MS experience pain.
source: It is well known that many patients with MS experience pain (Thompson et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2010.

claim: The proportion of patients with a progressive course of MS trend higher among patients with chronic types of pain.
source: Kalia and O'Connor found that the proportion of patients with a progressive course of MS trend higher among patients with chronic types of pain (Kalia and O'Connor, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kalia and O'Connor, 2005.

claim: Central pain is the first and sole symptom of MS relapse in some patients (1.6% of all patients, 6% of patients with central pain).
source: It was also reported that central pain is the first and sole symptom of MS relapse in some patients (1.6% of all patients, 6% of patients with central pain) (Osterberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Osterberg et al., 2005.

claim: Several reports have failed to show a clear relationship between pain and disease duration and/or course in MS.
source: At the same time, several reports have failed to show a clear relationship between pain and disease duration and/or course (Beiske et al., 2004; Kalia and O'Connor, 2005; Michalski et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Beiske et al., 2004; Kalia and O'Connor, 2005; Michalski et al., 2011.

claim: There does not seem to be a direct correlation clinically between pain intensity and MS disability or lesional load.
source: Thus, there does not seem to be a direct correlation clinically between pain intensity and MS disability or lesional load.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cited literature.

claim: Loss of pain sensitivity may vary with the region or size of the affected site between MS patients, such that a bigger affected site correlates with less sensitivity.
source: It is known that loss of pain sensitivity may vary with the region or size of the affected site between patients, such that a bigger affected site correlates with less sensitivity in MS patients (Huber et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Huber et al., 1988.

claim: Depression occurs with high frequency in MS patients.
source: In addition, depression occurs with high frequency in MS patients (Chwastiak et al., 2002; Siegert and Abernethy, 2005), and this might also affect sensation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chwastiak et al., 2002 and Siegert and Abernethy, 2005.

claim: Depression in MS patients might affect sensation.
source: In addition, depression occurs with high frequency in MS patients (Chwastiak et al., 2002; Siegert and Abernethy, 2005), and this might also affect sensation.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation.

claim: Depression in MS patients also affects the sympathetic pathway.
source: Moreover, depression in MS patients also affects the sympathetic pathway (Guinjoan et al., 1995; Rumsfeld and Ho, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Guinjoan et al., 1995 and Rumsfeld and Ho, 2005.

claim: At least three factors are important for determining the sites of relapse in MS patients: (1) the existence of excess MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at a particular site, (2) activation of a sympathetic pathway that accumulates MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in certain blood vessels, and (3) the presence of organ-specific autoreactive CD4+ T cells in the periphery.
source: We propose at least three factors as important for determining the sites of relapse in MS patients: (1) the existence of excess MHC class II+CD11b+ cells at a particular site, (2) activation of a sympathetic pathway that accumulates MHC class II+CD11b+ cells in certain blood vessels, and (3) the presence of organ-specific autoreactive CD4+ T cells in the periphery.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal in the Discussion.

claim: Even when MHC class II+CD11b+ cells are accumulated in specific vessels, inflammation is not induced without autoreactive CD4+ T cells, which recognized some autoantigens on the accumulated MHC class II+CD11b+ cells.
source: Even when MHC class II+CD11b+ cells are accumulated in a specific vessels, the inflammation is not induced without autoreactive CD4+ T cells, which recognized some autoantigens on the accumulated MHC class II+CD11b+ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion.

claim: The sites of excess MHC class II+CD11b+ cells and sympathetic activations vary among MS patients as too the antigens recognized by autoreactive T cells, which would explain the variation in MS relapse regions.
source: We assume the sites of excess MHC class II+CD11b+ cells and sympathetic activations vary among patients as too the antigens recognized by autoreactive T cells, which would explain the variation in MS relapse regions.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption in the Discussion.
